items.title: MIT study: 'attribution decay' makes large diffusion models' outputs untraceable to specific training images
items.summary_en: MIT CSAIL researchers Zheng Dai and David Gifford report that as diffusion-model training datasets scale up, the influence of any single training example on a given generated output shrinks toward zero, a phenomenon they term 'attribution decay.' Using data-ablation experiments, they found that at sufficiently large scale, removing a specific image, an artist's entire body of work, or all photos of a given person from the training set often does not change what the model generates. The paper, 'Outputs of Generative Diffusion Models Are Often Unattributable,' is reported to be forthcoming in Nature Communications.
items.notes: Peer-reviewed venue reported (Nature Communications, forthcoming) — not a preprint. Relevant to ongoing debates about copyright/attribution in generative AI training data; direct csail.mit.edu fetch was blocked in this run, content corroborated via a mirrored MIT EECS listing and independent tech press coverage (The Register, InfoWorld).
